If this is an excerpt that is fine, but if it is meant to stand alone it feels thin.

drafts.note: The core thesis lands well and the three-characteristic frame (high-volume, deterministic, verifiable) is the strongest part of the piece - it gives readers something concrete to test their own ideas against, and it earns the confident tone in the closing paragraph. "We expect significant disruption to the incumbent vertical SaaS industry, deep changes to commercial models, and strong winner-takes-most dynamics" is three large claims in one sentence and none of them are developed - the commercial model shift in particular (seat-based to outcome-based, presumably) is the most interesting part of the thesis and deserves its own paragraph. Similarly, "We've made 15 investments in this category over the past two years" is doing a lot of credibility work but a reader has no idea whether that means USD 5 million or USD 500 million of deployed capital, or what any of the companies look like. One named portfolio example would make the whole piece land harder. Also worth reconsidering the US/UK spelling mix ("labour", then presumably US readership) - pick a lane.

I would also push back on calling 300-400 bps of margin uplift plus 9% revenue growth plus M&A plus operating leverage a plan that nets to only 2.4x and 19% - either the bridge is conservative and worth saying so, or something is being double-counted, and a sentence reconciling the pillars to the return would preempt the question.

A sharper close tying back to why we win at this price would lift the whole piece.

Finally, the closing on 2026 realizations is thin given its importance; at minimum the reader will want a sense of expected proceeds range or multiple, even if caveated.
